title: Here’s Why There Aren’t Any Tiny Dinosaurs
gist: Non-avian dinosaurs bottomed out at just under a pound — bunny-sized — even though birds and lizards routinely miniaturize to under 2 grams, and a new study in Evolution takes on why that size floor existed. The piece is a short news teaser that sets up the question without reporting the study’s answer.

insights.claim: Argentinosaurus weighed more than 80 tons, making it the most massive animal ever to walk the Earth and anchoring the popular association of dinosaurs with extreme body size.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Baseline number for any size-evolution or biomechanics argument about terrestrial vertebrate maxima.
insights.quote: Argentinosaurus, for example, was the most massive animal ever to walk the face of the Earth, weighing more than 80 tons.

insights.claim: The smallest known non-avian dinosaurs weighed a little less than a pound — roughly rabbit-sized — which is large compared with how small vertebrates can actually get.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: The claim of interest is not that dinosaurs were big but that their lower bound was unusually high.

insights.claim: The bee hummingbird, a living avian dinosaur, weighs under 2 grams and would be dwarfed by the smallest non-avian dinosaur, showing the lineage could miniaturize once it became birds.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Constraint on dinosaur body size was lineage- and era-specific, not a hard vertebrate physics limit.

insights.claim: The dwarf gecko, the world’s smallest lizard, fits on a fingertip with room to spare, demonstrating that other reptile lineages solved miniaturization that non-avian dinosaurs never did.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Comparative benchmark that sharpens the puzzle the new study addresses.
